title: no-exposed-unauthenticated-service
description: >-
  Publishing Ollama, Qdrant, or the Docker MCP gateway on all host interfaces without authentication lets anyone on the network use it. How to bind to loopback instead.
---

A `ports` entry such as `11434:11434` publishes the container on every network interface of the host. For most services that is a deliberate choice. For some AI services it opens a door with no lock, because the service has no authentication to fall back on. This rule reports a service that runs one of these images, publishes a port on all interfaces, and sets nothing in Compose that turns authentication on.

- **Ollama** has no server authentication, and its official image sets `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434`, so a published port is reachable from the whole network.
- **Qdrant** listens on `0.0.0.0` by default, and its `api_key` is commented out. The rule treats `QDRANT__SERVICE__API_KEY` in `environment` as authentication.
- **The Docker MCP gateway** creates a bearer token by default. The rule reports it only when `command` contains `--allow-unauthenticated`.

The rule reads `ports` in the short and the long syntax. It reports an entry with no host address and an entry bound to `0.0.0.0` or `[::]`. A `${BIND:-0.0.0.0}` address resolves to its default. A `${BIND}` address with no default is unknown, so the rule does not report it. `network_mode: host` counts as published. `expose` does not, because it never opens a port on the host. The rule matches the image name and skips a service with `build:`, since its `image:` value is only a tag.

## What the rule catches

```yaml title="compose.yaml — Ollama on every host interface"
services:
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:0.12.3
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
```

Scanning this file reports:

```text
⚠ WARN [docker-doctor/no-exposed-unauthenticated-service]
  Service 'ollama' publishes Ollama on all interfaces, and Ollama has no authentication here. Anyone who can reach this host can use it.
```

## Why it matters

These services hand over real capability and real data. Anyone who reaches Ollama can run prompts on your hardware, pull models, and delete the ones you installed. Anyone who reaches Qdrant can read and overwrite every collection, which in an agent stack is its memory. Anyone who reaches the MCP gateway can call every tool behind it, including tools that act with your stored secrets and OAuth tokens. [CVE-2026-76092](https://github.com/docker/mcp-gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-g879-4j4f-6vj7) describes exactly that for a gateway in a container, and its workaround is to bind the port to loopback or a trusted network. Loopback is not the whole answer for the gateway. [CVE-2025-64443](https://github.com/docker/mcp-gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-46gc-mwh4-cc5r) is a DNS rebinding flaw that lets a web page in your browser reach a gateway running in SSE or streaming mode, which the gateway fixed in v0.28.0. Keep the port off the network first, and keep the gateway current.

## How to fix it

Bind the port to loopback (`127.0.0.1:11434:11434`), or drop `ports` and reach the service over an internal network, or put an authenticating proxy in front of it.

```yaml title="compose.yaml — loopback bind and an internal network"
services:
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:0.12.3
    ports:
      - 127.0.0.1:11434:11434
  qdrant:
    image: qdrant/qdrant:v1.15.0
    networks:
      - backend
  app:
    image: my-app:1.2.0
    networks:
      - backend

networks:
  backend:
    internal: true
```

Pick the fix that matches how the service is used:

- **Bind the port to loopback.** `127.0.0.1:11434:11434` keeps the service reachable from the host and closes it to the network.
- **Drop `ports` and use an internal network.** Services on the same Compose network reach each other by name, and `internal: true` stops the network from routing outside.
- **Turn authentication on.** Set `QDRANT__SERVICE__API_KEY` for Qdrant, and leave `--allow-unauthenticated` off for the gateway.
- **Put an authenticating proxy in front.** Ollama has no authentication of its own, so a reverse proxy that checks a key is the way to share it.

The list holds only products whose default bind and authentication were confirmed in the product's own source or documentation. A missing product does not mean it is safe, only that the rule has not verified it.

Docker publishes ports through its own firewall rules, which run before host firewalls such as ufw. A ufw deny rule does not close a published port, so do not treat the host firewall as the fix.

The rule reads only the `environment` and `command` of the service. A Qdrant key that arrives through `env_file` or a mounted config file is not seen, and the rule still reports the service. Gateway releases from 0.25.0 up to 0.43.0 served no authentication in container mode at all, whatever the flags said, so pin 0.43.1 or later.

A monitoring or lab host that is meant to serve its whole network can set this rule to `off` in `docker-doctor.config.json`.

## Rule details

- **Rule key** — `docker-doctor/no-exposed-unauthenticated-service`
- **Category** — Compose
- **Default severity** — `warning`
- **Applies to** — Docker Compose files

Explain this rule from the CLI:

```bash
npx @docker-doctor/cli@latest rules explain docker-doctor/no-exposed-unauthenticated-service
```

Change its severity — or turn it off — in your [config file](/docs/reference/configuration):

```ts
// docker-doctor.config.ts
export default {
  rules: {
    "docker-doctor/no-exposed-unauthenticated-service": "off",
  },
};
```

Severity affects the [health score](/docs/reference/scoring): `error` findings cost more points than `warning`, and `info` costs the least.
